title: Steerling-8B-Instruct: Our Inherently Interpretable Instruct Model
summary: We are releasing the instruction-following variant of Steerling, which preserves the base model's interpretability.
body_markdown:
We are releasing Steerling-8B-Instruct, the instruction-following variant of our interpretable base model, which we[previously announced](https://www.guidelabs.ai/post/steerling-8b-base-model-release/) . This model retains all the interpretability properties the base model was trained to have, while also supporting multi-turn dialogues. It is now used in production on[Clarity](https://www.guidelabs.ai/post/meet-clarity/) , our inherently interpretable AI platform. In this post, we cover how we trained the model and provide a checklist for others who want to perform instruction supervised fine-tuning (ISFT).


Steerling is a block-causal diffusion language model. The open-source model with the architecture closest to ours is LLaDA , which is also a diffusion-based language model. Although LLaDA uses a full-attention mask rather than Steerling’s block-causal mask, the instruction supervised fine-tuning (ISFT) pipeline should be the same. To ensure we could reliably instruction-tune diffusion-based models, we first reproduced LLaDA’s SFT results to verify that our pipeline worked, then applied it to our own Steerling model.


## Reproducing LLaDA ISFT


As a first step, we reproduced the LLaDA-8B instruction supervised fine-tuning (ISFT) setup . The paper includes some important details, but we uncovered many additional details while reproducing the results. This section discusses our findings.


### Data and Tokenization


Unfortunately, the LLaDA ISFT dataset is not publicly available. However, we found that[allenai/tulu-3-sft-olmo-2-mixture](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/tulu-3-sft-olmo-2-mixture) , the same dataset used for ISFT of OLMo 2 , is sufficient to reproduce the English-language benchmark results. Based on the number of observations reported in the LLaDA paper , we trained for four epochs on this dataset.


To tokenize multi-turn dialogues, we apply the LLaDA template . This is essentially the Llama-3 template , but without a beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, as diffusion models do not need one. The template looks like this:


```text
<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>\n\n{system}<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>\n\n{user}<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>\n\n{assistant}<|eot_id|>
```


where` <|start_header_id|>` ,` <|end_header_id|>` , and` <|eot_id|>` are special tokens.


LLaDA then unfolds the multi-turn dialogues: given pairs of user ( ui\\textbf{u}_i


) and assistant ( ai\\textbf{a}_i


) messages, an observation of {u1,a1,…,uI,aI}\\{\\textbf{u}_1, \\textbf{a}_1, \\dots, \\textbf{u}_I, \\textbf{a}_I\\}


becomes \[{u1,a1},{u1,a1,u2,a2},⋯ ,{u1,a1,…,uI,aI}\]\[\\{\\textbf{u}_1, \\textbf{a}_1\\}, \\{\\textbf{u}_1, \\textbf{a}_1, \\textbf{u}_2, \\textbf{a}_2\\}, \\cdots, \\{\\textbf{u}_1, \\textbf{a}_1, \\dots, \\textbf{u}_I, \\textbf{a}_I\\}\]


. Because LLaDA is not a causal model, unfolding is required for prompts containing only part of a dialogue to be in-distribution. For example, if the model had been trained without unfolding, providing only {u1,a1,t}\\{\\textbf{u}_1, \\textbf{a}_{1,t}\\}


for t>0t > 0


(meaning a1,t\\textbf{a}_{1,t}


is partially masked) would be out-of-distribution, because the model would expect some of u2\\textbf{u}_2


to be provided as well.


### Checklist


When reproducing results, we often find that there is no special trick or magic hack that makes things work. It’s often just a matter of pursuing correctness at a level of detail that can seem obsessive. Sometimes, fixing one issue can make the model’s accuracy worse, but once you fix all the issues, things start to work. It can be hard to identify all these issues, but over time, we have developed a useful checklist.


-


**Support special tokens in the prompts.**


Users can ask questions like:


> Write a multi-turn LLM template using the special tokens` <|start_header_id|>` and` <|end_header_id|>` .


If you use Hugging Face’s default[apply_chat_template](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/chat_templating) behavior, it will encode` <|start_header_id|>` and` <|end_header_id|>` as special tokens. This undermines the meaning of the special tokens, as users should not be able to insert them directly into their prompts. Instead,` <|start_header_id|>` should be parsed as regular tokens, for example` \['<|', '#start', '#_header', '#_id', '#|>'\]` . That way, the model can learn to copy these tokens while still understanding where each message starts and ends. Unfortunately,` apply_chat_template` doesn’t support this kind of parsing, so it’s often necessary to implement your own template serializer using the[split_special_tokens=True](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/main_classes/tokenizer#transformers.TokenizersBackend) feature in Hugging Face’s tokenizer.


-


**Use global shuffling and shuffle independently each epoch.**


Some dataloaders split the dataset into shards and then shuffle each shard independently. This makes the sampling less i.i.d. both within and across epochs. In our[dataloader article](https://www.guidelabs.ai/post/dataloader-how-we-built/) , we discuss the consequences of not using global shuffling and explain how we implemented it.


-


**Checkpointing must be exact.**


If you are using checkpointing, which you should for multi-day runs, it’s essential that the logic for resuming training is exact. For example, you must not skip, reorder, or duplicate observations. Many training frameworks do not handle this reliably.


-


**Randomly initialize new token embeddings to different values.**


When adding special tokens, you need to extend the embedding matrix and language model head. These additional weights need to be randomly initialized. We find that the exact initialization method is not so important. However, it’s easy to forget to initialize the weights, leaving them at zero or giving each new token the same initial embedding. These initialization patterns do not work as well as random initialization.


-


**Only assign loss to predicted tokens.**


During pretraining, all output tokens contribute to the loss, and this pattern is often carried over into post-training. However, we find that assigning loss only to predicted tokens significantly improves benchmark results. This means user-context tokens, assistant tokens from previous model responses, and header tokens such as` <|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>\\n\\n` should not be assigned a loss, as they are never predicted.


-


**Aggregate the loss using sums.**


In textbooks and simple training implementations, we often learn to take the mean of the loss to normalize its scale. However, in distributed ISFT settings, taking the sum is usually preferable. This is because the number of tokens varies across observations in ISFT. Since the mean is computed per GPU, each GPU’s loss is normalized by a different factor:


∑i=1GPUs∑j∈MiLj∣Mi∣≠∑i=1GPUs∑j∈MiLj∑j∈Mi∣Mi∣\\sum_{i = 1}^{GPUs} \\sum_{j \\in M_i} \\frac{\\mathcal{L}_{j}}{|M_i|} \\not= \\sum_{i = 1}^{GPUs} \\frac{\\sum_{j \\in M_i} \\mathcal{L}_{j}}{\\sum_{j \\in M_i} |M_i|}


This unequal normalization can reduce accuracy, and the simplest fix is to sum the losses instead. The OLMo 2 team reported similar results . A natural concern is whether this requires adjusting the learning rate. Adam is invariant to constant rescaling, and gradient norm clipping is also invariant when the gradient exceed the clipping threshold. These properties typically mean the learning-rate does not need to be modified.


-


**Inspect benchmark outputs using the benchmark harness.**


So far, the checklist has focused on training. However, even with fully correct training, issues with the benchmark harness can still reduce measured accuracy. For example, in the MBPP benchmark , we found that the model would output the correct implementation but leave a space before` def` , causing a syntax error.


```text
def   replace_char  (  string  ,   old  ,   new  ):
return   string.replace(old, new)
```


On further investigation, we found that all the in-context examples had a similar space, so the model was actually following the instructions correctly. The root cause turned out to be[lm-evaluation-harness](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness) , which hardcodes a space whenever a generation prefix is provided. Some models ignore this space in the examples, while others follow the examples closely and reproduce it. Removing this hardcoded space increased benchmark accuracy from 0% to 39%.

We did not include HellaSwag, as it is a likelihood benchmark that LLaDA adapted for multiple-choice generation, which is somewhat awkward. If it were included, the averages would be 53.82%, 53.57%, and 53.48%, respectively.


## From LLaDA to Steerling


Training the Instruct version of Steerling is similar to training LLaDA. We use the same template, unfolding procedure, and general checklist to ensure correctness. However, while we were reproducing LLaDA’s results with the Tulu 3 dataset, the Dolci dataset was released, so we switched to it for Steerling. There are also some significant changes because Steerling uses block-causal diffusion and is inherently interpretable.


### Block-causal diffusion and interpretability changes


Unlike LLaDA, Steerling uses block-causal diffusion. While LLaDA pads sequences with end-of-sequence tokens (` \[EOS\]` ) to make them equal in length, we effectively pad only the last diffusion block that contains content (the finalizer block) with` \[EOS\]` tokens. Tokens after the finalizer block are never predicted. Therefore, in line with the checklist, these tokens should not contribute to the loss.


A significant difference between LLaDA and Steerling is that Steerling is inherently interpretable. We achieve this by annotating the dataset with concepts and applying a number of interpretability losses. This process is essentially the same in ISFT as in pretraining, so we will not go into detail about the annotations and losses here. You can read[Scaling Interpretable Language Models to 8 Billion Parameters](https://www.guidelabs.ai/post/scaling-interpretable-models-8b/#training-objectives) and[The FineWeb Concept Atlas](https://www.guidelabs.ai/post/the-fineweb-concept-atlas/) for those details.


ISFT does introduce some significant differences, though. Like the language model loss, the interpretability losses are applied only to the tokens we predict: the assistant tokens in the last message. However, we still want to support masking any input token to enable input-attribution explanations. We achieve this by applying diffusion masking to all input tokens, including both user and assistant message tokens, rather than just the predicted tokens in the last assistant message. The same trick works for LLaDA, and we found no performance penalty on average.

### Performance benchmarks


Here we compare Steerling’s benchmark results with those of other models. Steerling does not perform quite as well as some newer models, as discussed in[Steerling-8B: The First Inherently Interpretable Language Model](https://www.guidelabs.ai/post/steerling-8b-base-model-release/) . This is because Steerling was pretrained with significantly fewer resources than other models, which are overtrained. When we account for this by plotting performance against pretraining FLOPs, Steerling performs as expected.

### Interpretability metrics


During post-training, we apply the same interpretability losses used during pretraining and mid-training, as described in[Scaling Interpretable Language Models to 8 Billion Parameters](https://www.guidelabs.ai/post/scaling-interpretable-models-8b/#training-objectives) . It is therefore natural to compare interpretability metrics across these training stages. Unfortunately, this is not straightforward. The validation metrics used during pretraining and mid-training are based on natural text continuations. However, the post-trained model is instruction-tuned and will not continue an input in the same way as a model from either earlier stage. To bridge this gap, we prompt the model with` Continue the following text: {text}` , then treat the assistant’s output in the same way as the output from the earlier models. This comparison is imperfect, but it allows us to use the same dataset.


**Concept losses:** When we evaluate the interpretability losses on a validation dataset, we find that the concept loss, which measures concept-classification accuracy, remains unchanged, while the independence loss increases.

**Concept contribution:** Despite the increase in independence loss, when we examine the output contributions from known concepts, discovered concepts, and the residual stream, we find that the contribution from known concepts has increased, while the residual contribution has decreased. Overall, this suggests that post-training has improved our concept attribution and ability to steer the model.

**Known concept alignment:** Finally, we measure concept alignment by comparing concept attributions with assessments from an LLM judge. We find that concept alignment has also improved.

Overall, post-training yields mostly identical or slightly better results on interpretability metrics. One possible explanation is that concepts are less ambiguous in an instruction-following context than in a pure text-continuation context.


### Release


Our Steerling-8B-Instruct model, the first inherently interpretable large language model, is now in production on[Clarity](https://www.guidelabs.ai/post/meet-clarity/) . We have also made it available for anyone to use on Hugging Face at[guidelabs/steerling-8b-instruct](https://huggingface.co/guidelabs/steerling-8b-instruct) .
